edition.fomc: Next: 9–10 Dec (25bp hike ~99%; multiple Fed officials flagged urgency; Waller suggested large hike may be needed; labour data the swing factor for 50bp)
edition.stripNote: Mon 23 Nov. Friday's session featured a dramatic late reversal in crude oil — Brent surged in the final hour on renewed Iran escalation concerns, settling at $92.57 per barrel (+0.65%) after trading as low as $89.80; WTI settled at $83.98. The previous edition captured prices before this reversal. Gold fell for a tenth consecutive session to $3,532, a 14-month low, as Fed rate-hike odds for December held at 99% and the dollar held near 19-month highs. Silver declined 4.1% to $41.50. The equity correction deepened — the VIX reached a 7-month high; Anthropic (ANT) fell 9% to $88.30 in its second session. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.95% on flight-to-safety buying. Copper fell to $5.52/lb ($12,160/t LME); platinum $1,295; palladium $895. Coal held at $150. Over the weekend, Bitcoin staged a sharp recovery from $58,200 to approximately $60,900 after hitting a low near $55,640 on Saturday; Ethereum recovered to $1,718. Ukrainian naval drones struck six commercial vessels in the Black Sea, sinking two — a major maritime escalation alongside the ongoing Hormuz threat (JMIC threat: severe; traffic 65% below pre-conflict levels). The November 27 gallium/germanium/antimony deadline is now 4 days away — the G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus on critical minerals, leaving no major diplomatic venue before the deadline. LME base metals: nickel $15,310, zinc $3,503, tin $41,160. Corn at 4-month low 434½¢; wheat 574¼¢; soybeans 1,220¾¢. LNG JKM rose to $30/MMBtu.

overview: Friday's session featured dramatic late reversals that the previous edition's prices did not fully capture. Brent crude surged in the final hour on renewed Iran escalation concerns, settling at $92.57 per barrel — up 0.65% — after trading as low as $89.80 intraday. WTI settled at $83.98. The oil reversal was the standout exception in an otherwise brutal risk-off session. Gold fell for a tenth consecutive session to approximately $3,532 per ounce, a 14-month low, as Fed rate-hike odds for December held at 99% and the dollar remained near 19-month highs. Silver declined 4.1% to $41.50. The equity correction deepened: the Dow and S&P 500 remained in correction territory, the Nasdaq sat in its third correction of 2026, and the VIX reached a 7-month high. Anthropic (ANT) fell 9% to $88.30 in its second trading session. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.95% as flight-to-safety bond buying offset rate-hike expectations. Copper fell 2.9% to $5.52 per pound ($12,160 per tonne LME). Platinum declined 3.4% to $1,295; palladium fell 2.1% to $895. Newcastle coal held at $150. Corn remained at a 4-month low of 434½ cents; wheat at 574¼ cents; soybeans at 1,220¾ cents.

Over the weekend, Bitcoin staged a sharp recovery from Friday's crash — rebounding from an intraday low near $55,640 on Saturday to approximately $60,900 by Sunday evening, up roughly 2% over the latest 24 hours. Ethereum recovered to $1,718 from $1,597. In the Black Sea, Ukrainian naval drones struck six commercial vessels over the weekend in one of the most significant maritime escalations of 2026, sinking two and disrupting grain and oil export routes from Russian and Ukrainian ports. Combined with continued Hormuz attacks — where JMIC rates the threat as severe and traffic remains 65% below pre-conflict levels — global maritime trade now faces a dual-theatre shipping threat. The November 27 deadline for China's export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 4 days away with no extension announced. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta (October 31–November 1) ended without consensus on critical minerals, leaving no major diplomatic venue before the deadline. LME base metals were weaker on Friday: nickel settled at $15,310 per tonne, zinc at $3,503, and tin at $41,160. LNG JKM rose to $30 per MMBtu as winter demand supports. Cocoa held at $5,294 on West African supply concerns. Lithium carbonate stabilised near ¥90,000 per tonne in China.

watchItems.title: November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline now 4 days away — no extension announced
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline for China's US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony is now 4 days away. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta (October 31–November 1) ended without consensus on critical minerals, leaving no major diplomatic venue before the deadline. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium, 60–80% of germanium, and close to half of mined antimony. Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus approximately $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing. If the bans resume on Thursday, Western semiconductor and defence supply chains face renewed disruption.

watchItems.title: Dual maritime threat — Black Sea drone strikes sink 2 vessels; Hormuz attacks continue; global shipping under pressure
watchItems.text: Ukrainian naval drones struck six commercial vessels in the Black Sea over the weekend, sinking two in one of the most significant maritime escalations of 2026. Grain and oil export routes from Russian and Ukrainian ports are disrupted. Combined with the Strait of Hormuz threat — where a tanker was hit on Friday (the seventh strike in a week), JMIC rates the threat as severe, and traffic remains 65% below pre-conflict levels — global maritime trade now faces a dual-theatre shipping threat. The Hormuz paradox persists: despite surging attacks, Middle East crude exports have returned toward pre-war levels. The Black Sea disruption has more direct implications for grain exports — Russia and Ukraine together account for roughly 25% of global wheat exports.

watchItems.title: Oil reverses on Friday — Brent settles at $92.57 as Iran concerns trump recovering Middle East exports
watchItems.text: Brent crude reversed sharply higher in the final hour of Friday's session, settling at $92.57 per barrel — up 0.65% — after trading as low as $89.80. The previous edition captured prices before this reversal. Reports of renewed Iranian military activity near the Strait triggered late buying. WTI settled at $83.98. The reversal underscores the fragility of the oil price: recovering Middle East export flows have been pushing prices lower, but any escalation signal can reverse the trend instantly. Combined with the Black Sea maritime disruption over the weekend, the energy supply picture is becoming more complex heading into the November 27 deadline.

watchItems.title: Bitcoin stages weekend recovery — rebounds from $55,640 low to $60,900 as dip buyers emerge
watchItems.text: Bitcoin staged a sharp weekend recovery from Friday's 8.8% crash, bouncing from an intraday low near $55,640 on Saturday to approximately $60,900 by Sunday evening. Ethereum recovered from $1,597 to $1,718. The recovery came as dip buyers emerged across crypto markets. However, the Fear and Greed Index remains in Extreme Fear territory. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows have exceeded $2.5 billion in 2026. The key question is whether the recovery holds into Monday's trading session, with equities still in correction territory, the VIX at a 7-month high, and December rate-hike odds at 99%. A sustained reclaim of $60,000 would signal the worst of the crypto sell-off may have passed.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: 10th consecutive decline · 14-month low · down ~8% on the week — worst in 8 months · 10Y yield fell to 4.95% · dollar at 19-month high · Dec hike odds 99%
desk.sum: Gold fell for a tenth consecutive session on Friday, dropping approximately 2.5% to $3,532 per ounce — a 14-month low and the longest losing streak in over a year. The relentless selling continued as CME FedWatch showed December rate-hike odds at 99% and the dollar held near its strongest level in 19 months. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.95% as flight-to-safety bond buying emerged amid the equity correction, though that was insufficient to support gold against the dominant rate-hike narrative. The sell-off is part of a broader risk-off liquidation that has pushed the Dow and S&P 500 into correction territory. Gold is down approximately 8% on the week — its worst weekly performance in eight months. Key support at $3,500.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Sharp decline · gold-silver ratio ~85 · down ~25% over past month · first dip below $42 since early 2026 · industrial exposure amplified sell-off
desk.sum: Silver fell 4.1% to $41.50 per ounce on Friday, one of the worst-performing commodities of the session. The intraday low reached $40.99 — the first dip below $41 in months. Silver's dual precious-industrial profile made it especially vulnerable as both yield-driven precious metal selling and risk-off industrial demand concerns compounded. The gold-silver ratio narrowed slightly to approximately 85. Silver has declined roughly 25% over the past month, with the sell-off accelerating as December rate-hike odds hit 99% and the Nasdaq entered correction territory. The break below $42 opens support at $40–$41.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $83.98 · dramatic late-session reversal on Iran concerns · intraday low $89.80 · Black Sea: 6 vessels struck · dual shipping threat · ME exports recovering
desk.sum: Brent crude reversed sharply higher in the final hour of Friday's session, settling at $92.57 per barrel — up 0.65% — after trading as low as $89.80 intraday. Reports of renewed Iranian military activity near the Strait of Hormuz triggered late buying that overwhelmed the earlier sell-off. WTI settled at approximately $83.98. The reversal underscores the fragility of oil prices: recovering Middle East export flows have been pushing crude lower, but any escalation signal can reverse the trend instantly. Over the weekend, Ukrainian naval drones struck six commercial vessels in the Black Sea, sinking two — adding a second theatre of maritime disruption to the energy supply picture. The dual shipping threat could support prices heading into the November 27 deadline.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$12,160/t · continued losses · dollar near 19-month high · DRC logistics disruption ongoing · Chinese physical premiums at records
desk.sum: Copper fell 2.9% to $5.52 per pound (approximately $12,160 per tonne LME official settlement) on Friday, extending losses in the broader risk-off sell-off. The dollar near 19-month highs remains the dominant headwind. Chinese physical premiums have hit record levels even as LME prices decline, signalling divergence between financial and physical markets. The DRC bridge collapse continues to disrupt logistics. AI data-centre, EV and electrification demand remain structural long-term drivers, but the hostile macro environment caps near-term upside. Key support at $5.40 per pound ($11,900 per tonne).

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~40% YTD · held steady again · winter demand · LNG supply crisis continues · no Hormuz deal · Indonesia coal ~$145
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held at $150 per tonne on Friday, continuing to buck broader commodity weakness as winter demand and the Hormuz-driven LNG supply crisis sustain the thermal fuel bid. Coal is up approximately 40% year to date. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus on the Hormuz situation. QatarEnergy's force majeure continues through at least end-December 2026. Indonesian coal trades near $145 as mining demand builds. The energy supply crisis and coal-to-gas substitution dynamics remain supportive through winter.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Sharp decline · sold off with broader precious metals · EV shift weighing · South African supply constrained · yields headwind easing slightly
desk.sum: Platinum fell 3.4% to $1,295 per ounce on Friday, caught in the broad precious metals sell-off. The EV transition continues to pressure automotive catalyst demand. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues. With the dollar near a 19-month high and December rate-hike odds at 99%, the macro environment is hostile, though the 10-year yield falling to 4.95% on flight-to-safety buying provides a marginal offset. Hydrogen electrolysis demand provides a structural long-term floor but cannot offset near-term selling pressure.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Deep below $900 · down ~35% YoY · EV transition headwind dominant · weakest sustained level since 2018
desk.sum: Palladium fell 2.1% to $895 per ounce on Friday, remaining below the psychologically significant $900 level for the first time since 2018. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — continues to dominate. With the dollar near 19-month highs, yields at 4.95% and December rate-hike odds at 99%, the macro environment remains hostile. Tight South African mine supply offers limited support. The break below $900 is technically significant and opens the next support zone around $870–$880.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: Tanker hit by projectile Fri · 7 strikes on 6 vessels in past week · traffic 65% below pre-conflict · JMIC threat: SEVERE · 3 US carriers in Gulf · Black Sea adds 2nd theatre
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October. A tanker was hit by a projectile near Khasab, Oman on Friday — the seventh strike in the region in a week. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, with two seafarers missing and 13 injured. JMIC rates the threat as severe with further deliberate attacks highly likely. Combined Hormuz traffic is about 65% below pre-conflict levels. The paradox persists: despite surging attacks, Middle East crude exports have returned toward pre-war levels, though oil reversed higher late on Friday on renewed Iran concerns. The US is widening its blockade of Iranian ship-to-ship transfers. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf. Meanwhile, Ukrainian naval drones struck six vessels in the Black Sea over the weekend, sinking two — global maritime trade now faces a dual-theatre shipping threat.

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: At 4-month low · down 11¢ on the week · dollar strength persists · Black Sea attacks disrupt grain routes · South American planting favourable
desk.sum: December corn held at a 4-month low of 434½ cents per bushel as of Friday's close, down 11 cents on the week as dollar strength continued to weigh on US export competitiveness. The broader risk-off sell-off added to pressure across agricultural commodities. Over the weekend, Ukrainian naval drones struck six commercial vessels in the Black Sea, sinking two — disrupting grain export routes from Russian and Ukrainian ports. This could support US corn export competitiveness if Black Sea disruption persists. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the November WASDE report provides a structural floor. Key support at 430 cents.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Continued decline · down 19¢ on the week · Black Sea attacks disrupt grain exports · SovEcon Russia estimate supports floor
desk.sum: December SRW wheat held at 574¼ cents per bushel as of Friday's close, down 19 cents on the week. HRW wheat at 624½ cents. The sell-off was broad-based amid the risk-off environment. Over the weekend, Ukrainian naval drones struck six commercial vessels in the Black Sea, sinking two — a significant disruption to grain export routes. Russia and Ukraine together account for roughly 25% of global wheat exports, so sustained Black Sea disruption could provide a floor or push prices higher. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes — below the USDA's forecast — provides additional structural support. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for US competitiveness.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month ~$12.21 · rebounded Fri · down 10¾¢ on the week · Black Sea disruption may support · South American supply competitive
desk.sum: January soybeans held at 1,220¾ cents per bushel as of Friday's close, one of the few commodities to end the session higher as bargain buying emerged after the week's heavy selling. Soybeans are still down 10¾ cents on the week. The weekend's Black Sea maritime escalation — with Ukrainian drones striking six vessels and sinking two — could support US soybean export competitiveness if disruption persists. South American supplies remain more competitive at current exchange rates. No progress has been visible on the Busan truce soybean commitments through any diplomatic channel. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for US exports.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,718 · weekend recovery from $55,640 low · reclaimed $60K · spot ETF outflows >$2.5B in 2026 · Fear & Greed still Extreme Fear
desk.sum: Bitcoin staged a sharp weekend recovery, rebounding from an intraday low near $55,640 on Saturday to approximately $60,900 by Sunday evening — up roughly 2% over the latest 24 hours. Ethereum recovered from $1,597 to $1,718. The recovery came as dip buyers emerged following Friday's 8.8% crash. Bitcoin's reclaim of $60,000 is a constructive signal, though the Fear and Greed Index remains in Extreme Fear territory. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows have exceeded $2.5 billion in 2026. The key test comes Monday when equity markets reopen: the VIX at a 7-month high, the Nasdaq in correction, and December rate-hike odds at 99% present continued headwinds. A sustained hold above $60,000 would suggest the worst of the sell-off has passed.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM Dec contract ~$30 · TTF ~$30 · HH ~$3.35 · QatarEnergy FM continues · EU storage ~70% — 20% below 5Y avg · oil reversal supports LNG
desk.sum: The Asian LNG spot JKM December contract has risen to approximately $30 per MMBtu, up from $29, as winter demand intensifies. TTF sits near $30 per MMBtu; Henry Hub near $3.35. EU gas storage at approximately 70% is roughly 20% below the five-year average heading into winter — the thinnest in a decade. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026. Friday's oil reversal to $92.57 supports the case for sustained LNG pricing strength. Over 60 bcm of Qatari and UAE loadings have been lost between March and October. US LNG export feedgas hit a record 19.3 bcf per day.
desk.src: S&P Global Platts · Global LNG Hub · JOGMEC

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · 3 carriers in Gulf · tanker hit Fri · 7 strikes in a week · 4 days to Nov 27 deadline · oil reversal signals continued supply stress
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October, with a tanker hit on Friday — the seventh strike in a week. Despite recovering crude export flows, sulfur supply logistics remain disrupted. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Friday's oil reversal to $92.57 on Iran concerns underscores the fragility of supply recovery. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 4 days away, adding to supply-chain uncertainty. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus, leaving no diplomatic venue before the deadline.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · wheat & corn weakness weighing on fertiliser sentiment · Black Sea disruption adds logistics risk
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Wheat and corn both declining on the week, with corn at a 4-month low, is modestly negative for near-term fertiliser demand sentiment. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The weekend's Black Sea maritime escalation — six vessels struck, two sunk — adds logistics risk to potash trade routes from the region.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 4 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · no progress from any diplomatic channel · ban resumption increasingly priced in
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The November 27 deadline is now 4 days away with no extension announced. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus on critical minerals, leaving no major diplomatic venue before the deadline. Market participants are increasingly pricing in ban resumption. If the deadline passes without extension, overseas prices could spike further. China produces close to half of global mined antimony.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 4 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · no progress from any channel · ban resumption increasingly priced in
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. The November 27 deadline is now 4 days away with no extension announced. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus on critical minerals — no major diplomatic venue remains before the deadline. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium and 60–80% of germanium. The underlying licensing regimes remain in force during the suspension. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing. Ban resumption is increasingly priced in.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Steady at $5.30 · upstream tightness · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ · Nov 27 deadline 4 days
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness. The November 27 deadline, now 4 days away, affects the broader critical minerals complex. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus on critical minerals. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Rebounded 2.4% · up from $5,063 on Thu · West African supply concerns reasserted · El Niño risk · $5,000 holding as support
desk.sum: ICE cocoa held at $5,294 per tonne as of Friday's close, having rebounded 2.4% and bucked the broader commodity sell-off as West African supply concerns reasserted themselves. The bounce from $5,063 on Thursday confirms the $5,000 level as strong psychological support. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projection that 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an exceptionally strong El Niño event continues to provide a medium-term bullish underpinning. Despite ICE warehouse inventories at a 2.5-year high of 3.8 million bags, the market remains focused on forward supply risks.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Continued decline from $33,525 · European demand concerns persist · Rotterdam $16–17/lb · DRC bridge disruption ongoing · NMC-to-LFP shift weighing
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $33,000 per tonne, continuing to decline as European demand concerns persist. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $16–17 per pound. The DRC bridge collapse continues to have secondary effects on cobalt logistics, with alternative routes adding time and cost. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift weighs on the structural demand outlook. The dollar near 19-month highs adds to the headwinds for an already-weak market. The broader risk-off sell-off on Friday further dampened industrial metals sentiment.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Stabilising near ¥90,000 · InfoLink reported 7.2% fall in Nov · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate is stabilising near ¥90,000 per tonne after the sharp sell-off earlier in November. InfoLink reported a 7.2% fall in lithium carbonate prices in early November, driven by expected mine supply recovery and weaker residential demand. Structural oversupply remains the dominant theme, with Goldman Sachs projecting a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Supply ramp-ups in Australia and South America continue to outpace demand growth. The ¥85,000 zone represents next major support.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil reversal pressures synthetic costs higher
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Friday's oil reversal to $92.57 modestly increases synthetic rubber production costs, tilting the balance slightly in favour of natural rubber. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The dollar near 19-month highs remains a headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot held above $90 · term price $98/lb near record · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · miners sliding 23% while prices hold · AI demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds near $91 per pound U₃O₈, with long-term contract prices at $98 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. Despite spot prices holding above $90, uranium miners (URNM ETF) have slid approximately 23% year to date, reflecting rate sensitivity, contract-price lag and ETF-driven selling. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide. Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant delays continue to limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Down ~2.6% in Nov · ex-China NdPr slipping below $110/kg · Nov 27 deadline 4 days · prices fell sharply on Nov 20 sell-off
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide has declined approximately 2.6% in November to around $71 per kilogram domestically in China. SMM reported that prices fell sharply on November 20 amid broader market selling. Ex-China NdPr prices are slipping below the $110 per kilogram support level as oversupply builds. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony — now 4 days away — adds uncertainty to the broader critical minerals complex. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus. Downstream magnetic material orders remain weak and buyers are cautious about high-priced inventory.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat · broader metals sell-off weighing
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption and the broader commodity sell-off cap near-term gains. Friday's risk-off environment had no direct impact on manganese pricing but adds to the bearish sentiment for industrial metals.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: LME official settlement · down from $15,400 · Indonesian RKAB uncertainty persists · global surplus continues · macro headwinds dominant
desk.sum: LME nickel settled at $15,310 per tonne on Friday, declining approximately 0.9% as macro headwinds reasserted in the risk-off sell-off. Indonesian RKAB mining quota uncertainty persists — potential tightening provides a floor while the global nickel surplus from Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions caps upside. The dollar near 19-month highs remains the primary headwind. The Dow and S&P 500 in correction territory and the VIX at a 7-month high added to the negative sentiment across industrial metals. Key support at $15,000.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: LME official settlement · continued decline · Myanmar ban constraining supply · macro sell-off dominant · LME backwardation wide
desk.sum: LME tin settled at $41,160 per tonne on Friday, declining approximately 2.1% as the sell-off across base metals continued. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The LME backwardation remains wide, signalling tight near-term supply. However, macro pressure from the strong dollar, rising rate-hike expectations and the broader equity correction continues to overwhelm supply-side support. The November 27 deadline, now 4 days away, adds geopolitical uncertainty to the broader metals complex.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: LME official settlement · 5-day losing streak extends · TCs deeply negative · structural deficit intact · macro headwinds dominant
desk.sum: LME zinc settled at $3,503 per tonne on Friday, declining approximately 1.7% and extending a five-day losing streak amid the broad risk-off sell-off. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments outside China. The structural supply deficit remains intact despite near-term macro pressure. Zinc is still up approximately 15% year-over-year. The dollar near 19-month highs remains the primary headwind. The equity correction and VIX at a 7-month high added to the negative industrial metals sentiment.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,750 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 4 days to Nov 27 deadline · no progress from any diplomatic channel
desk.sum: European tungsten APT holds at $2,750 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu — Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. The November 27 deadline is now 4 days away with no extension announced. The G20 Finance Ministers meeting in Atlanta ended without consensus on critical minerals, leaving no diplomatic venue before the deadline. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls. If the bans resume on Thursday, the Western premium could widen further.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · 7 Hormuz strikes in past week · tanker hit Fri · exports recovering but attacks surging
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The Strait of Hormuz saw its most active week of attacks since mid-October — a tanker was hit on Friday, the seventh strike in a week. Despite the sustained attacks, Middle East crude exports are recovering toward pre-war levels, though helium supply logistics from Qatar remain disrupted. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years. Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium. Russia's export controls extend through 2027. The November 27 deadline is 4 days away with no diplomatic progress.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · corn & wheat weakness negative for fertiliser demand
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Corn at a 4-month low and wheat's continued decline are modestly negative for near-term fertiliser demand sentiment.
